title: DOJ Sues to Block Alaska Senate Certification if Sullivan Loses
excerpt: The Justice Department argues a second candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan could confuse voters in a ranked-choice race that may decide Senate control, and asks a court to halt certification pending an investigation.
body:
• The Justice Department sued Alaska on October 22, asking a federal court to block certification of the state's U.S. Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses and the result may have been affected by voter confusion.
  • The case centers on a second candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher whose presence on the November 3 ballot the DOJ calls a frivolous candidacy meant to benefit Democrat Mary Peltola.
  • Alaska uses ranked-choice voting: if no candidate wins a majority of first-choice votes, the lowest candidate is eliminated and ballots are redistributed until a winner emerges. Tabulation is expected to start November 18.
  • For voters in Alaska and across the U.S., the suit tests whether a federal court can delay a state from certifying a Senate result before any votes are counted.

The Trump administration's Justice Department has filed a preemptive lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from certifying its U.S. Senate election if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses, arguing that a second candidate with a nearly identical name could confuse voters and change the outcome. The suit, filed October 22 in federal court in Alaska, asks the court to declare unlawful any result "impacted by voter confusion" and to stop state officials from certifying it until an investigation determines whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant for Senator Sullivan, according to CNN and USA Today.

The race could decide control of the Senate: Democrats need to net four seats in November, and Alaska is one of the Republican-held states they hope to flip. Also on the ballot are Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher from Petersburg, and Republican Gerald Heikes.

What the Lawsuit Argues

The Justice Department contends Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy exists to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing votes for Senator Sullivan. It says the challenger is a longtime supporter of Democratic candidates, registered as a Republican when he filed, and that his campaign website uses a format, color scheme and theme similar to the senator's campaign site. The complaint invokes the National Voter Registration Act, citing the law's stated purpose "to protect the integrity of the electoral process."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=cYucExJac74

"The United States likewise suffers an injury when the certification of the election for a federal office is tainted by a frivolous candidacy because that undermines confidence in the make-up and workings of the federal government."

— U.S. Department of Justice lawsuit

President Donald Trump previewed the move earlier this week in a Truth Social post, writing that having a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot amounted to cheating. "It's ridiculous that the Court didn't stop this SCAM. Even 1, 2, or 3% could make the difference," Trump wrote, according to CNN. At a rally this month in Wasilla, Alaska, he said, "It's just cheating. They found a guy named Dan Sullivan. They put him up to get a little confused."

Context and Background

Alaska election officials initially sought to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot. A trial court rejected that effort, and in June the Alaska Supreme Court ruled he should remain on the ballot. On the ballot itself, officials listed the incumbent as Dan S. Sullivan, identified as a registered Republican and as the incumbent, while Daniel J. Sullivan appears without a party affiliation, using middle initials to separate the two names.

https://x.com/CNN/status/2113656037660041434

In the primary, the incumbent won 68,726 votes and Daniel J. Sullivan won 4,107, CNN reported. Under Alaska's system, the top four primary finishers advance regardless of party, and voters rank candidates in order of preference. Daniel J. Sullivan has said he chose to run on his own, the Associated Press reported. Neither Alaska's Division of Elections nor the Peltola campaign immediately responded to requests for comment, USA Today reported.

Impact and Analysis

Election law experts were sharply skeptical. Derek Muller, a professor at Notre Dame Law School, called the department's legal argument "one of the worst ones I've ever seen" and said the department was plucking language from the preface of the voter registration law to claim a free-wheeling right to enjoin a state's election operations. He also noted that because ballots are co-mingled, it is unclear how an investigation could identify which voters cast a ballot for a Sullivan they did not intend.

"This is friendly fire, this is suing Republicans in Alaska, I don't know that is going to be taken by state officials."

— Derek Muller, Notre Dame Law School

Ben Ginsberg, a former top election counsel to the Republican National Committee, told CNN a federal court is unlikely to grant what the administration wants, partly because courts should not change voting policies close to an election. "There is not a rational legal reason to do it," Ginsberg said.

What's Next

The case has been assigned to Judge Sharon L. Gleason, an appointee of President Barack Obama, and the administration has not yet sought emergency action. Alaska officials expect to begin ranked-choice tabulation on November 18, after the deadline for overseas ballots to arrive. A ruling before then would determine whether certification can proceed on schedule if Sullivan loses.
